paras: The killing of Alfred Perry was the fatal shooting of Perry, a Black man, by James Thorp, a workman in the Missouri Pacific railroad machine shops, at Kansas City, Missouri, on Sunday, August 22, 1880. Thorp was arrested; the wire dispatch said Perry had first made, or tried to make, an assault on him with rocks. The next afternoon, during Perry's funeral, a large Black crowd chased a man described as Thorp's brother-in-law, and white packing-house workers threatened to drive the city's Black residents into the river. The shooting ran as a brief wire item in papers across the country, while the funeral disturbance drew a separate dispatch to the Chicago Tribune.

According to a Kansas City dispatch dated August 23, Thorp and Perry had an "altercation" the day before, and after Perry "had made, or attempted to make an assault on him with rocks," Thorp shot him four times, killing him almost instantly. A shorter Times special said Thorp shot Perry for "attempting to throw stones" during the quarrel. Neither dispatch named a witness for the rock-throwing, and no account from Perry's side appears in the reports. Thorp was arrested, and the Chicago Tribune placed the killing "down in West Kansas."

On the afternoon of August 23, during funeral services over Perry's body, word spread that John Moffatt, whom the Tribune called the killer's brother-in-law, had made "some foul remark." The mourners left the funeral and chased Moffatt nearly ten blocks, throwing brickbats and stones, while he fled with a pistol in each hand and fired several shots. The Tribune put the crowd at "over 1,000" and said it was trying to lynch Moffatt; police arrived and had a hard struggle to keep him from the crowd. The chase ended near the large packing houses, where more than 200 butchers turned out and "threatened to drive every negro into the Missouri River." Further trouble was expected, and a large police force guarded the area.

Beyond Thorp's arrest, no report of an inquest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage. As late as September 3, a Minnesota criminal calendar still described the case only as a shooting "during an altercation."

Most white papers printed the Kansas City dispatch in a few lines inside crime roundups, next to a Pleasant Hill store shooting and a Burlingame, Kansas, saloon killing, under headings such as "Kansas City Tragedies" and "Wicked Western Ways." Headlines split on the killing itself: the Wheeling Register ran it as "Wouldn't Be Stoned. A White Man Shoots a Negro at Kansas City," taking up the shooter's account, while the Daily Kennebec Journal headed its one-line version "Negro Murdered." News summaries in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and the Daily Republican reduced the case to a single sentence.

The Chicago Tribune's special, headed "An Angry Mob," said Thorp had "murdered" Perry but described the funeral crowd as "half-drunken, howling negroes." Three days later the Corvallis Gazette in Oregon condensed the Tribune story, naming Moffatt as Perry's killer and moving the threatened drowning to the Mississippi. All of the coverage came from white papers; no Black newspaper account of the killing appears.

The victim appears as Alfred Perry in most reports, as "Fred Perry" in the Times special and as "Alfred Terry" in the Daily Republican. The Tribune called the killer "Alfred Thorp," and the Corvallis Gazette said Moffatt "killed the negro" Perry, but the Corvallis item condensed the Tribune dispatch, which names Moffatt only as the brother-in-law, and every other report names James Thorp. Dispatches dated August 23 placed the shooting "yesterday" and the Tribune on Sunday, while the one-line Kennebec Journal item said "to-day."

reader.title: Killing of Alfred Perry
bases: A single workman shot a Black man after a quarrel and was arrested; no mob, band or officers took part in the killing (A2, A7), and the next day's crowd chase and threats are reported as its aftermath (A4).
The Kansas City wire dispatch (A2, A7), a separate Times special (A1) and the Chicago Tribune's own special (A4) agree that James Thorp killed Perry at Kansas City.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the dispatch in a few lines in crime roundups ('Kansas City Tragedies', 'Wicked Western Ways', 'Fatal Feuds in Kansas'), giving the rock-throwing claim as part of the story.
The Wheeling Register headlined it 'Wouldn't Be Stoned. A White Man Shoots a Negro at Kansas City.'
The Daily Kennebec Journal headed its line 'Negro Murdered.'
The Chicago Tribune said Thorp 'murdered' Perry but headlined the funeral crowd 'An Angry Mob' of 'half-drunken, howling negroes.'

conflicts.note: Most reports, including the fuller wire dispatch, give Alfred Perry; the variants look like transmission or typesetting errors.
The Corvallis item is a later condensation of the Tribune dispatch, which names Moffatt only as the killer's brother-in-law; every other report names James Thorp.
The one-line Kennebec item is the outlier; the fuller dispatches and the Tribune agree on Sunday.
The Tribune original names the Missouri; the Corvallis condensation changed it.

record_check.dossier: The shooting was on Sunday, August 22 (Aug. 23 dispatches say 'yesterday'); the funeral and crowd chase were on August 23.
